children.name: idempotent
children.comment:
Worst case on a retry: the recipient gets the same welcome email twice —
never a reason to let a maintenance-interrupted or transiently-failed
delivery dead-letter permanently instead of trying again. Without this,
platform.go's worker safeguard refuses every retry past the first with
"cannot redeliver non-idempotent intent", including the very retry the
maintenance-hold pattern below depends on.

The worker/schedule/webhook-trigger entry points bypass the HTTP
maintenance middleware entirely — this guard is what makes maintenance
mode apply to them too. See internal/ops.MaintenanceGate.RegisterAction.

children.name: message
children.raw: "maintenance mode is on; welcome delivery is paused"

children.comment:
Circuit breaker around the outbound call: "breaker-guard" refuses to
even attempt it while the circuit is open (protecting a struggling
dependency from every replica's retries, not just slowing each one
down with its own timeout); "delivery-ok"/"breaker-record" report the
real outcome back regardless of success or failure, and
"delivery-succeeded" re-raises a failed delivery as this intent's own
failure — on_error "continue" on "deliver" only ever exists to let the
breaker observe the failure; it must never be the thing that decides
whether this intent succeeded, or a struggling notification service
would make notify.welcome report success anyway and this worker's
retry (bcl/05_workers.bcl, max_attempts 5) would never fire.

children.comment:
The shape check IS the conditional gate here: validate.schema fails
(422) rather than denying, and every node below that `requires
[validated]` (directly or transitively) simply never runs if it does.

--- The branch ---------------------------------------------------------
`flow.branch` evaluates each case's `condition` in order (over the fact
named by `input_fact`, "input" by default) and runs the first match's
`intent` as a child intent — a genuinely separate, independently
testable graph, not an inline branch of this one. `default_intent` runs
when nothing matches; `required false` would let it publish nothing
instead of failing. It publishes `{outcome, case, result}`: `case` is
the matched case's name, `result` is that child intent's own response.

children.name: cases

children.comment:
--- The business rule ---------------------------------------------------
A `kind decision` node denies the same way auth.require_session does:
`!Allowed` fails this node, and "insert" below (which requires
policy_decision) never runs — no separate validate.expression gate
needed, unlike ops.maintenance_status's `bool` fact. See
rules/orders/policy.bcl for the policy and why it's a second engine
rather than another flow.branch case.

requires [input] only, deliberately not [input, validated]: "validated"
has no speculation, so its own node cannot run until every decision
node in this intent has resolved (execution/scheduler.go's
isGateEligible — a plain node without post_policy_safe/pre_auth_safe
waits on the full decision verdict). Adding "validated" here would
make this decision node depend, transitively, on a fact that itself
waits on this decision node completing — a real bug, not a slow path:
with "validated" in requires, every /api/v1/orders POST was denied
(generic "access denied", no node past auth.require_session ever ran)
regardless of amount. Verified by reproducing it before landing the
fix without "validated" here.

children.comment:
The table. Each rule's `condition` sees `order` (the row just loaded)
and `input` (the request); `flags.priority_shipping` is available here
exactly like it is in any other expression in this document. A rule
further down the list only matters if every rule above it missed, so
the priority-shipping rule for "pending -> paid" is listed before the
plain one for the same pair — otherwise the plain rule would always win.

children.name: rules
children.raw:
[
        { name "pay_priority" condition "order.status == 'pending' and input.status == 'paid' and flags.priority_shipping and order.amount > 500" outcome "apply_priority" reason "paid with priority shipping" },
        { name "pay" condition "order.status == 'pending' and input.status == 'paid'" outcome "apply" reason "paid" },
        { name "ship" condition "order.status == 'paid' and input.status == 'shipped'" outcome "apply" reason "shipped" },
        { name "deliver" condition "order.status == 'shipped' and input.status == 'delivered'" outcome "apply" reason "delivered" },
        { name "cancel" condition "order.status != 'delivered' and input.status == 'cancelled'" outcome "cancel" reason "cancelled before delivery" }
      ]

children.name: description
children.raw: "Create a draft todo — a plain row insert; nothing durable starts until todo.submit"

children.comment:
The wire format is flat (title, description, assignee_email, priority,
due_date as direct top-level fields) — matching every other form this
starter posts (register, login, orders — see
resources/templates/pages/todos/new.html), and matching what a plain
<form method="POST"> actually sends: a native HTML form has no way to
produce a nested JSON body, and application/x-www-form-urlencoded
parsing (platform/routes.go) builds a flat map from form field names,
one level only, no dotted-key nesting.

Two independent validate.schema checks against that same flat input,
not one shape nesting "details"/"assignment" as sub-objects — found the
hard way while building this. The natural-looking design (a "todo_input"
shape composing both group shapes, one data.transform reshaping the
flat body to match before validating) turns out not to work with this
platform's current data.transform: neither a dotted extract target
(`details.title "input.title"`) nor a nested set block
(`set { details { title "..." } } }`) actually produces correctly
nested, templated output — the BCL block decoder nests a dotted extract
key into a sub-map that Extract's own `map[string]string` can't read
back out, and a nested set sub-block's string values never reach `{{ }}`
template rendering at all (only Set's own top-level string values do).
This starter's own end-to-end test caught it immediately: the create
form 422'd on the very first real submission. validate.schema tolerates
fields a shape doesn't declare (confirmed directly against a running
server before relying on it), so checking the same flat object against
two independent shapes is both simpler and actually correct — no
reshaping step to get wrong, and todo_details/todo_assignment are still
two independently meaningful, independently reusable validation groups,
each still driving its own <fieldset> in
resources/templates/pages/todos/new.html. The grouping was never really
about object nesting on the wire.
An unfilled <input type="email">/<input type="date"> still submits as
an empty string, not an absent field — browsers don't omit unfilled
optional fields from a form post. todo_assignment's `format
email`/`format date` checks reject "" (a real, present value, just not
a valid email/date), even though neither prop is `required` — confirmed
directly: the create form 422'd on exactly this ("assignee_email must
be an email address") the first time it was tested with only the
required title filled in, the single most common real submission.
`null` reads as genuinely absent to a format check (still doesn't
satisfy `required true`, which title alone needs); flat, non-dotted
extract keys are the mechanism proven to work above.

children.name: statement
children.raw: "INSERT INTO todos (owner_id, title, description, assignee_email, priority, due_date, status) VALUES ($1, $2, $3, $4, COALESCE($5, 'medium'), $6, 'draft') RETURNING id, owner_id, title, description, assignee_email, priority, due_date, status, run_id, created_at, updated_at"
children.comment:
COALESCE(..., 'medium'), not just the column's own DB-level default:
a browser form always submits every field it has, even an unfilled
<select> (which still has whatever option is marked `selected` —
"medium" here — so priority is realistically never actually blank
from this form), but a bare API caller could still omit it
entirely, and an explicit NULL bypasses a column default (a column
default only fires when the column is left out of the INSERT
altogether) — priority has no nullable escape hatch the way
assignee_email/due_date do.
